title: Διομήδης Ὀδυσσέα αἱρεῖται
source: Homer, The Iliad, Greek text of D. B. Monro and T. W. Allen, Homeri Opera, tomi I–II, 3rd ed. (Oxford Classical Texts; Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1920), public domain; TEI from PerseusDL/canonical-greekLit tlg0012.tlg001.perseus-grc2, sha256 ae8b617018c6e5af. Text as printed: the edition sets no quotation marks round speeches, and none are added. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca — an admitted convention; Homer's own pronunciation was older and is not recoverable in detail. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; ï for a separately sounded ι; accents omitted). Scansion: made by program from the text and checked; it shows one defensible reading of each line, and the notes say where a line is irregular. All translations were made fresh from the Greek for Lectorium.
about: Nestor leads the kings across the ditch to a clear space where the ground shows free of the dead, and there proposes that a man go among the Trojans to learn their plans; he promises fame and a black ewe with a lamb from every chief. All fall silent until Diomedes volunteers, asking for a companion, and many rise: the two Ajaxes, Meriones, Nestor’s son, Menelaus and Odysseus. Agamemnon tells Diomedes to choose whom he likes and not to pass over the better man out of respect for rank (he fears for Menelaus); Diomedes chooses Odysseus, who declines praise and says the night is two parts gone. They arm, Diomedes with Thrasymedes’ sword, shield and bull’s-hide helmet, Odysseus with Meriones’ bow, quiver, sword and a helmet set with boar’s tusks, once stolen by Autolycus. As they set out, Athena sends a heron on the right that they only hear in the dark, and each prays to her, Diomedes promising a heifer with gilded horns.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπὼν τάφροιο διέσσυτο·
sentences.tr: hōs eipōn taphroio diessyto·
sentences.l: So having spoken, he darted across the ditch;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and darted across the ditch;
sentences.n: The speaker is Nestor, who has just finished telling the guards to keep watch (the last words of the previous part). ὣς εἰπών ‘so having spoken’ closes that speech. διέσσυτο is the aorist of διασεύομαι ‘dart across’, without the augment, and τάφροιο is an epic genitive in -οιο (= -ου), here ‘across the ditch’, the ditch the Achaeans dug in front of their wall. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) inside the line. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο
Ἀργείων βασιλῆες ὅσοι κεκλήατο βουλήν.
sentences.tr:
toi d’ ham’ heponto
Argeiōn basilēes hosoi keklēato boulēn.
sentences.l:
and with him followed
the kings of the Argives, as many as had been called to the council.
sentences.i: and the kings of the Argives who had been summoned to the council followed with him.
sentences.n: τοὶ δ’ ἅμ’ ἕποντο: τοί is the old demonstrative (= Attic οἱ) ‘they’, and ἕποντο is the imperfect of ἕπομαι ‘follow’ without augment; ἅμ’ is ἅμα ‘along with’ (him). The kings are named at once as Ἀργείων βασιλῆες ‘kings of the Argives’. κεκλήατο is the epic pluperfect passive of καλέω in the form ‘they had been called’, and βουλήν is an accusative of the thing to which they were called, ‘to the council’.

sentences.t:
τοῖς δ’ ἅμα Μηριόνης καὶ Νέστορος ἀγλαὸς υἱὸς
ἤϊσαν·
sentences.tr:
tois d’ hama Mērionēs kai Nestoros aglaos huios
ēïsan·
sentences.l:
And with them Meriones and the splendid son of Nestor
went;
sentences.i: Meriones went with them, and so did Nestor’s splendid son;
sentences.n: τοῖς δ’ ἅμα ‘and along with them’ looks back to the kings; Μηριόνης is the Cretan Meriones, Idomeneus’ companion. Νέστορος ἀγλαὸς υἱός ‘Nestor’s splendid son’ is a name-epithet pair, and the son is not named here. ἤϊσαν is the imperfect plural of εἶμι ‘go’ (an Attic ᾖσαν), and its verb waits until the start of line 197, so the unit ends at the raised dot (·) in the middle of that line.

sentences.t: αὐτοὶ γὰρ κάλεον συμμητιάασθαι.
sentences.tr: autoi gar kaleon symmētiaasthai.
sentences.l: for they themselves called them to take counsel together.
sentences.i: for it was they themselves who had called them to take counsel together.
sentences.n: αὐτοί ‘they themselves’ is Nestor and the kings, and γάρ ‘for’ explains why these two young men were with the party: they were invited, not merely following. κάλεον is an uncontracted imperfect of καλέω ‘call’ (Attic ἐκάλουν), and συμμητιάασθαι is a rare epic infinitive of συμμητιάομαι ‘take counsel together’ (μῆτις is ‘cunning’, and the verb is built on it).

sentences.t:
τάφρον δ’ ἐκδιαβάντες ὀρυκτὴν ἑδριόωντο
ἐν καθαρῷ,
sentences.tr:
taphron d’ ekdiabantes oryktēn hedrioōnto
en katharōi,
sentences.l:
And the ditch, the dug one, having crossed over, they sat down
in a clear place,
sentences.i: They crossed the dug ditch and sat down in a clear place,
sentences.n: τάφρον … ὀρυκτήν ‘the dug ditch’ is the Achaean ditch, with the adjective ὀρυκτός ‘dug’ after its noun. ἐκδιαβάντες is an aorist participle of ἐκδιαβαίνω ‘cross out over’, and the accusative shows what they crossed. ἑδριόωντο is an epic imperfect of ἑδριάομαι ‘sit down’. ἐν καθαρῷ ‘in a clear place’ is the first half of the phrase that goes on into the next unit.

sentences.t:
ὅθι δὴ νεκύων διεφαίνετο χῶρος
πιπτόντων·
sentences.tr:
hothi dē nekyōn diephaineto chōros
piptontōn·
sentences.l:
where indeed of the dead showed through the ground,
of those falling;
sentences.i: where the ground showed through, free of the fallen dead;
sentences.n: The line ἐν καθαρῷ ὅθι δὴ νεκύων διεφαίνετο χῶρος stands also at 8.489, where Hector holds his assembly, and the English follows that unit’s reading: the ground showed through, free of the dead. διεφαίνετο is ‘showed through’, and χῶρος ‘ground, place’ is its subject. νεκύων ‘of the dead’ is read as a genitive of separation, the ground clear of them, and πιπτόντων ‘of those falling’ says which dead: the men who fell in the day’s fighting. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after πιπτόντων.

sentences.t:
ὅθεν αὖτις ἀπετράπετ’ ὄβριμος Ἕκτωρ
ὀλλὺς Ἀργείους,
sentences.tr:
hothen autis apetrapet’ obrimos Hektōr
ollys Argeious,
sentences.l:
from which turned back again mighty Hector,
destroying the Argives,
sentences.i: the place from which mighty Hector had turned back again, destroying Argives,
sentences.n: ὅθεν ‘from where’ is the relative that picks up the clear place. ἀπετράπετ’ is the aorist ἀπετράπετο ‘turned back’, from ἀποτρέπομαι, with its ending elided. ὄβριμος Ἕκτωρ ‘mighty Hector’ is a name-epithet pair and the house rendering is ‘mighty’. ὀλλύς is the participle of ὄλλυμι ‘destroy’, ‘destroying’, with the Argives as its object.

sentences.t: ὅτε δὴ περὶ νὺξ ἐκάλυψεν.
sentences.tr: hote dē peri nyx ekalypsen.
sentences.l: when night, indeed, covered all round.
sentences.i: when night closed around.
sentences.n: ὅτε δὴ ‘when indeed’ names the moment when Hector broke off, and περί … ἐκάλυψεν is a split compound, ‘covered round’, in which περί is an adverb and the aorist ἐκάλυψεν ‘covered’ stands apart from it (tmesis). The subject is νύξ ‘night’. The sense is that the dark ended the day’s fighting.

sentences.t: ἔνθα καθεζόμενοι ἔπε’ ἀλλήλοισι πίφαυσκον·
sentences.tr: entha kathezomenoi epe’ allēloisi piphauskon·
sentences.l: There, sitting down, they declared words to one another:
sentences.i: There they sat and spoke to one another:
sentences.n: ἔνθα ‘there’ is the clear place. καθεζόμενοι is the participle of καθέζομαι ‘sit down’, ἔπε’ is ἔπεα ‘words’ with its ending elided, and ἀλλήλοισι is the dative ‘to one another’. πίφαυσκον is the imperfect of πιφαύσκω, a reduplicated form of φαύσκω ‘make known’, and it means ‘were telling, were declaring’. The line ends at the raised dot (·), and the next line names the first speaker.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ μύθων ἦρχε Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ·
sentences.tr: toisi de mythōn ērche Gerēnios hippota Nestōr·
sentences.l: And among them of speeches made-beginning the Gerenian horseman Nestor:
sentences.i: The Gerenian horseman Nestor was the first to speak among them:
sentences.n: The speech-introduction formula, the one that opens a speech after a gathering has sat down. τοῖσι is ‘to them, among them’, μύθων ἦρχε ‘began the speeches’ (ἄρχω with a genitive), and the name-epithet is Γερήνιος ἱππότα Νέστωρ: ἱππότα is an old nominative in -ᾱ (= ἱππότης), and the meaning of Γερήνιος is disputed (a place, Gerenia, or a word related to γέρων ‘old man’), so the English leaves it as a name.

sentences.t:
ὦ φίλοι οὐκ ἂν δή τις ἀνὴρ πεπίθοιθ’ ἑῷ αὐτοῦ
θυμῷ τολμήεντι μετὰ Τρῶας μεγαθύμους
ἐλθεῖν,
sentences.tr:
ō philoi ouk an dē tis anēr pepithoith’ heōi autou
thymōi tolmēenti meta Trōas megathymous
elthein,
sentences.l:
“O friends, would not some man be persuaded
by his own enduring heart
to go among the great-hearted Trojans,
sentences.i: “My friends, is there no man who would let his own enduring heart persuade him to go among the great-hearted Trojans,
sentences.n: Nestor makes the proposal that leads to the whole expedition. ὦ φίλοι is ‘O friends’, and οὐκ ἂν δή τις ἀνὴρ πεπίθοιθ’ is a question that expects yes, ‘would not some man be persuaded’: ἂν with the optative πεπίθοιθ’ (aorist middle optative of πείθω; the middle, ‘be persuaded’, takes the dative) marks a polite wish. ἑῷ αὐτοῦ θυμῷ τολμήεντι is ‘his own enduring heart’, with αὐτοῦ ‘of himself’ strengthening ἑῷ. θυμός is ‘heart’ here, and τολμήεις is ‘enduring’. Τρῶας μεγαθύμους ‘great-hearted Trojans’ is a stock pair. The infinitive ἐλθεῖν ‘to go’ opens the purposes that follow.

sentences.t: εἴ τινά που δηΐων ἕλοι ἐσχατόωντα,
sentences.tr: ei tina pou dēïōn heloi eschatoōnta,
sentences.l: if some one of the enemy he might catch lying at the edge,
sentences.i: to catch one of the enemy lying at the edge of their lines,
sentences.n: εἴ τινά που … ἕλοι is a condition in the optative that works as a purpose, ‘in case he might catch’: τινά ‘someone’, που ‘perhaps’, and ἕλοι the aorist optative of αἱρέω ‘take, seize’. δηΐων is the genitive plural of δήϊος ‘hostile’, used as a noun, ‘of the enemy’, and ἐσχατόωντα is the accusative singular of the participle of ἐσχατάω ‘lie at the edge’. The man at the edge is the straggler or outpost, who can be seized and questioned.

sentences.t: ἤ τινά που καὶ φῆμιν ἐνὶ Τρώεσσι πύθοιτο,
sentences.tr: ē tina pou kai phēmin eni Trōessi pythoito,
sentences.l: or some talk among the Trojans he might hear,
sentences.i: or hear some talk among the Trojans,
sentences.n: A second aim joined by ἤ ‘or’ to the first. φῆμιν is the accusative of φήμη (epic φῆμις) ‘talk, report’, and ἐνὶ Τρώεσσι is ‘among the Trojans’ (ἐνί with the epic dative in -εσσι). πύθοιτο is the aorist middle optative of πυνθάνομαι ‘learn, hear’. πύθοιτο also governs the two indirect questions in the lines that follow, which say what is to be learned.

sentences.t: ἅσσά τε μητιόωσι μετὰ σφίσιν,
sentences.tr: hassa te mētioōsi meta sphisin,
sentences.l: what things they are planning among themselves,
sentences.i: what they are planning among themselves,
sentences.n: ἅσσα is the neuter plural relative ‘what things’, an epic form (= ἅτινα), and τε is a particle that adds nothing to the sense. μητιόωσι is the third plural present of μητιάω (= μητιάομαι) ‘plan, devise’, built on μῆτις; μετὰ σφίσιν ‘among themselves’ uses the dative of the pronoun σφεῖς. This is an indirect question, the first of two the man is to find out.

sentences.t:
ἢ μεμάασιν
αὖθι μένειν παρὰ νηυσὶν ἀπόπροθεν,
sentences.tr:
ē memaasin
authi menein para nēusin apoprothen,
sentences.l:
or whether they are eager
to stay here by the ships, far off,
sentences.i: or whether they are eager to stay here by the ships, far from the city,
sentences.n: ἢ … ἦε ‘or whether … or’ sets two choices. μεμάασιν is the third plural perfect of μαίομαι ‘be eager’ (the stem is μεμα-), and it takes the infinitive μένειν ‘to stay’. αὖθι ‘here, on the spot’, παρὰ νηυσίν ‘by the ships’ (epic dative plural in -σιν), and ἀπόπροθεν ‘far off’, that is, away from the city. The second choice follows in the next unit.

sentences.t:
ἦε πόλιν δὲ
ἂψ ἀναχωρήσουσιν,
sentences.tr:
ēe polin de
aps anachōrēsousin,
sentences.l:
or to the city
back they will withdraw,
sentences.i: or will withdraw again to the city,
sentences.n: ἦε is the epic form of ἤ, ‘or’. πόλιν δέ is πόλιν with the suffix -δε ‘to’, so ‘to the city’, and ἂψ ‘back’ is an adverb. ἀναχωρήσουσιν is the future of ἀναχωρέω ‘withdraw’, ‘they will withdraw’, in the second half of the question.

sentences.t: ἐπεὶ δαμάσαντό γ’ Ἀχαιούς.
sentences.tr: epei damasanto g’ Achaious.
sentences.l: since they have mastered the Achaeans.
sentences.i: now that they have mastered the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ … γ’ ‘since indeed’ (γε stresses the reason) gives the reason why the Trojans might think of going home. δαμάσαντο is an aorist middle of δαμάζω ‘subdue’, with the middle having an active sense (‘they have mastered’), and Ἀχαιούς is its object. This is Nestor’s guess at what the Trojans may be thinking after the day’s success.

sentences.t: ταῦτά κε πάντα πύθοιτο,
sentences.tr: tauta ke panta pythoito,
sentences.l: all this he would learn,
sentences.i: he would learn all this,
sentences.n: ταῦτά κε πάντα πύθοιτο: κε (= ἄν) with the optative πύθοιτο ‘he would learn’ picks up the wish of lines 204–210 and states its result. ταῦτα … πάντα ‘all these things’ means the two things asked: what the Trojans are planning, and where they mean to be. The unit ends at the comma after πύθοιτο.

sentences.t:
καὶ ἂψ εἰς ἡμέας ἔλθοι
ἀσκηθής·
sentences.tr:
kai aps eis hēmeas elthoi
askēthēs·
sentences.l:
and back to us come
unscathed;
sentences.i: and come back to us unscathed;
sentences.n: καὶ ἂψ εἰς ἡμέας ἔλθοι: ἂψ ‘back’, εἰς ἡμέας ‘to us’ (ἡμέας = ἡμᾶς, the epic form of the accusative), and ἔλθοι the aorist optative of ἔρχομαι. ἀσκηθής ‘unscathed’ describes the man and not the verb; it means untouched by harm. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after ἀσκηθής.

sentences.t:
μέγα κέν οἱ ὑπουράνιον κλέος εἴη
πάντας ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους,
sentences.tr:
mega ken hoi hypouranion kleos eiē
pantas ep’ anthrōpous,
sentences.l:
great would be for him an under-heaven fame
among all men,
sentences.i: he would win great fame under the whole sky, among all men,
sentences.n: μέγα κέν οἱ … κλέος εἴη is another optative with κέν (= ἄν): ‘great for him would be fame’. οἱ is the epic dative pronoun ‘for him’, and κλέος is ‘fame’. ὑπουράνιον ‘under heaven’ (ὑπό + οὐρανός) is a rare adjective that means the fame would reach as far as the sky does. ἐπ’ ἀνθρώπους ‘among men’ uses ἐπί with the accusative as ‘over, among’, and πάντας says all of them.

sentences.t: καί οἱ δόσις ἔσσεται ἐσθλή·
sentences.tr: kai hoi dosis essetai esthlē·
sentences.l: and a gift will be his, a good one;
sentences.i: and a good gift will be his;
sentences.n: καί οἱ δόσις ἔσσεται ἐσθλή: οἱ is ‘for him’, and the future ἔσσεται (the epic spelling of ἔσται, ‘will be’) changes from the optatives to a plain promise. δόσις is ‘a gift’, here a reward, and ἐσθλή is ‘good’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after ἐσθλή, and the line after gives the gift.

sentences.t:
ὅσσοι γὰρ νήεσσιν ἐπικρατέουσιν ἄριστοι
τῶν πάντων οἱ ἕκαστος ὄϊν δώσουσι μέλαιναν
θῆλυν ὑπόρρηνον·
sentences.tr:
hossoi gar nēessin epikrateousin aristoi
tōn pantōn hoi hekastos oïn dōsousi melainan
thēlyn hyporrēnon·
sentences.i: for every one of the best men who hold sway over the ships will give him a black ewe with a lamb at her side;
sentences.n: ὅσσοι … ἄριστοι ‘as many as are best’ is the relative clause, and ἐπικρατέουσιν ‘hold sway’ with νήεσσιν ‘over the ships’ (the epic dative plural of ναῦς) says what the best men do: they command. τῶν πάντων οἱ ἕκαστος means ‘of them all, to him each one’, with οἱ the dative ‘to him’ (the man who goes). ὄϊν … μέλαιναν θῆλυν ‘a black sheep, a female’ is the accusative of ὄϊς; ὑπόρρηνον has the usual explanation ‘with a lamb beneath her’ (ὑπό + ῥήν, an old word glossed as ‘lamb’), so a ewe with a lamb. The gift is given to the man who succeeds. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after ὑπόρρηνον.

sentences.t: τῇ μὲν κτέρας οὐδὲν ὁμοῖον,
sentences.tr: tēi men kteras ouden homoion,
sentences.l: to this no possession is like,
sentences.i: no possession is like it,
sentences.n: τῇ μὲν κτέρας οὐδὲν ὁμοῖον: τῇ is the demonstrative ‘to this’ (the gift), so the dative goes with ὁμοῖον ‘like’, ‘no possession is like it’. κτέρας is a rare word for something one owns and prizes, ‘a possession’ (it is the singular, where the plural κτέρεα is more usual), and μέν is a particle that sets this gift against what follows.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ δ’ ἐν δαίτῃσι καὶ εἰλαπίνῃσι παρέσται.
sentences.tr: aiei d’ en daitēisi kai eilapinēisi parestai.
sentences.l: and always at feasts and banquets it will be present.”
sentences.i: and it will always have its place at feasts and banquets.”
sentences.n: αἰεί ‘always’ and ἐν δαίτῃσι καὶ εἰλαπίνῃσι ‘at feasts and at banquets’: δαίς is ‘feast’ and εἰλαπίνη ‘banquet’, both with the epic dative plural in -ῃσι. παρέσται is the future of πάρειμι ‘be present’, and its subject is the ewe, the gift just described. Nestor’s speech, which offers the black ewes and the fame, ends here.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἄρα πάντες ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ara pantes akēn egenonto siōpēi.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they then all became still in silence;
sentences.i: So he spoke, and they all fell hushed and silent;
sentences.n: The formula that closes a speech and tells what the hearers did, the same Greek as at 3.95, where the edition ends the line with a raised dot, and its English is kept from there; the Odyssey has the line with οἱ for οἳ. ἔφαθ’ is ἔφατο ‘he spoke’, and ἀκὴν ἐγένοντο σιωπῇ is ‘they became hushed in silence’, with ἀκήν an adverb that goes with the verb ‘be’. The edition ends this line with a full stop and begins a new paragraph at the next line. No one answers at once.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: toisi de kai meteeipe boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: And among them spoke also Diomedes, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: And Diomedes, good at the war-cry, also spoke among them:
sentences.n: A whole-line speech introduction, with the same shape as the line for Menelaus at 3.96. καὶ μετέειπε ‘spoke also among them’ is the aorist of μετεῖπον, and βοὴν ἀγαθός ‘good at the war-cry’ is Diomedes’ stock epithet in the house rendering; βοήν is an accusative of respect.

sentences.t:
Νέστορ ἔμ’ ὀτρύνει κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ
ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων δῦναι στρατὸν ἐγγὺς ἐόντων
Τρώων·
sentences.tr:
Nestor em’ otrynei kradiē kai thymos agēnōr
andrōn dysmeneōn dynai straton engys eontōn
Trōōn·
sentences.i: “Nestor, my heart and my proud spirit urge me on to enter the army of the Trojans, men who are hostile and close at hand;
sentences.n: Diomedes volunteers first. ἔμ’ is ἐμέ ‘me’, the object of ὀτρύνει, which is singular because the two subjects, κραδίη ‘heart’ and θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ ‘proud spirit’, are taken together. The pair θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ keeps ‘spirit’ for the epithet, as in the Odyssey, ‘manly spirit’ in the literal line and ‘proud spirit’ in the free English. δῦναι is the aorist infinitive of δύω ‘enter’ and takes στρατόν ‘the army’ as its object; ἀνδρῶν δυσμενέων ἐγγὺς ἐόντων ‘of hostile men being near’ is a genitive that depends on στρατόν, and Τρώων ‘of the Trojans’ at the start of line 222 names those men. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after Τρώων.

sentences.t:
ἀλλ’ εἴ τίς μοι ἀνὴρ ἅμ’ ἕποιτο καὶ ἄλλος
μᾶλλον θαλπωρὴ καὶ θαρσαλεώτερον ἔσται.
sentences.tr:
all’ ei tis moi anēr ham’ hepoito kai allos
mallon thalpōrē kai tharsaleōteron estai.
sentences.l:
but if some other man would go with me,
there will be more comfort and more confidence.
sentences.i: but if another man would go with me, there will be more comfort and more confidence.
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ εἴ τίς μοι ἀνὴρ ἅμ’ ἕποιτο καὶ ἄλλος: ἀλλ’ ‘but’ turns from his own readiness to what he would wish; the condition εἴ … ἕποιτο is an optative, ‘if some man were to follow’, and μοι ‘with me’ is the dative that goes with ἕποιτο (ἅμα is an adverb here, ‘together’). καὶ ἄλλος ‘another besides’ means a second man besides himself. μᾶλλον θαλπωρή ‘more comfort’ and θαρσαλεώτερον, the comparative of θαρσαλέος ‘bold, confident’, are what ἔσται ‘will be’; the neuter θαρσαλεώτερον is ‘something more confident’, here ‘more confidence’. θαλπωρή is ‘comfort’ (related to θάλπω ‘warm’). The two lines make one unit because line 222 has no stop of its own.

sentences.t:
σύν τε δύ’ ἐρχομένω καί τε πρὸ ὃ τοῦ ἐνόησεν
ὅππως κέρδος ἔῃ·
sentences.tr:
syn te dy’ erchomenō kai te pro ho tou enoēsen
hoppōs kerdos eēi·
sentences.l:
for when two go together, and the one sees before the other
how there may be gain;
sentences.i: when two go together, one sees before the other how there may be gain;
sentences.n: The general truth that backs up his wish. σύν … ἐρχομένω is a dual participle in two words (tmesis for συνερχομένω) ‘two going together’, with δύ’ ‘two’, and the dual shows the pair. καί τε is a generalising ‘and indeed’; ὃ τοῦ is ὁ τοῦ ‘the one before the other’, and ἐνόησεν is an aorist that states what always happens (a gnomic aorist), ‘notices’. ὅππως is ὅπως ‘how’, κέρδος is ‘gain, advantage’, and ἔῃ is the subjunctive of εἰμί ‘there may be’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after ἔῃ.

sentences.t:
μοῦνος δ’ εἴ πέρ τε νοήσῃ
ἀλλά τέ οἱ βράσσων τε νόος, λεπτὴ δέ τε μῆτις.
sentences.tr:
mounos d’ ei per te noēsēi
alla te hoi brassōn te noos, leptē de te mētis.
sentences.l:
but if one man alone notices,
yet his mind is rather short, and thin his cunning.”
sentences.i: but if a man alone notices, yet his mind is rather short, and his cunning thin.”
sentences.n: μοῦνος δ’ εἴ πέρ τε νοήσῃ: μοῦνος is ‘alone’ (= μόνος), εἴ πέρ τε is ‘even if’, and the subjunctive νοήσῃ is ‘he notices, thinks of’ (νοέω). The clause waits for the line that follows to finish its sense, so the two lines make one unit. ἀλλά … οἱ βράσσων τε νόος: ἀλλά ‘yet’, οἱ ‘his’ (the dative of possession), and βράσσων, which is generally taken as the comparative of βραχύς ‘short’, so ‘rather short’; the form is irregular and the explanation is the usual one, not certain. λεπτὴ δέ τε μῆτις ‘and thin his cunning’ has λεπτή ‘thin, fine’ and μῆτις ‘cunning’. The speech ends at the full stop, the end of the argument for taking a companion.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἔθελον Διομήδεϊ πολλοὶ ἕπεσθαι.
sentences.tr: hōs ephath’, hoi d’ ethelon Diomēdeï polloi hepesthai.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and they wished, many of them, to follow Diomedes.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and many of them wished to follow Diomedes.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφαθ’, οἳ δ’ ἔθελον: ἔθελον is the imperfect of ἐθέλω ‘wish’, ‘they were willing’, and Διομήδεϊ is the dative with ἕπεσθαι ‘to follow’ (the infinitive of ἕπομαι). πολλοί ‘many’ stands apart from οἳ and names the many who offered. The edition begins a new paragraph here, and the next lines list the volunteers one by one.

sentences.t: ἠθελέτην Αἴαντε δύω θεράποντες Ἄρηος,
sentences.tr: ētheletēn Aiante dyō therapontes Arēos,
sentences.l: Wished the two Ajaxes, two attendants of Ares,
sentences.i: The two Ajaxes, attendants of Ares, wished it,
sentences.n: ἠθελέτην is a dual verb, ‘the two wished’, which agrees with Αἴαντε ‘the two Ajaxes’, a dual too; δύω is ‘two’. θεράποντες Ἄρηος ‘attendants of Ares’ is the house rendering, and Ἄρηος is the epic genitive of Ἄρης. The two Ajaxes are the usual pair, the son of Telamon and the son of Oileus. The line goes on with the list of volunteers.

sentences.t: ἤθελε Μηριόνης, μάλα δ’ ἤθελε Νέστορος υἱός,
sentences.tr: ēthele Mērionēs, mala d’ ēthele Nestoros huios,
sentences.l: wished Meriones, and greatly wished the son of Nestor,
sentences.i: Meriones wished it, and Nestor’s son wished it very much,
sentences.n: ἤθελε ‘wished’ is used again and again as the list goes on, an anaphora that shows the number of men. Νέστορος υἱός ‘Nestor’s son’ is the same unnamed son as at 196. Thrasymedes is named at 255, but Nestor has other sons, so the Greek leaves him open. μάλα … ἤθελε ‘greatly wished’ puts an extra push on this one.

sentences.t: ἤθελε δ’ Ἀτρεΐδης δουρικλειτὸς Μενέλαος,
sentences.tr: ēthele d’ Atreïdēs dourikleitos Menelaos,
sentences.l: and wished Atreus’-son, Menelaus famed-for-the-spear,
sentences.i: and Menelaus, the son of Atreus, famed for his spear, wished it,
sentences.n: Ἀτρεΐδης is a patronymic, ‘Atreus’ son’, and it fits both brothers, but the name Μενέλαος in the same line shows that it is Menelaus. δουρικλειτός is ‘famed for the spear’ (δόρυ + κλειτός), the house rendering of the epithet.

sentences.t:
ἤθελε δ’ ὁ τλήμων Ὀδυσεὺς καταδῦναι ὅμιλον
Τρώων·
sentences.tr:
ēthele d’ ho tlēmōn Odyseus katadynai homilon
Trōōn·
sentences.l:
and wished enduring Odysseus to enter the throng
of the Trojans;
sentences.i: and enduring Odysseus wished to enter the throng of the Trojans;
sentences.n: ὁ τλήμων Ὀδυσεύς: ὁ is the article, and τλήμων ‘enduring’ is the adjective from τλάω ‘endure’; it is kept apart from πολύτλας ‘much-enduring’. καταδῦναι is the aorist infinitive of καταδύω ‘go down into, enter’, and ὅμιλον ‘throng’ is its object. Τρώων ‘of the Trojans’ is placed at the start of 232, so the unit ends at the raised dot (·) after it.

sentences.t: αἰεὶ γάρ οἱ ἐνὶ φρεσὶ θυμὸς ἐτόλμα.
sentences.tr: aiei gar hoi eni phresi thymos etolma.
sentences.l: for always in his wits his heart was daring.
sentences.i: for the heart in his wits was always daring.
sentences.n: αἰεὶ γάρ ‘for always’ explains why Odysseus was among the volunteers. οἱ ἐνὶ φρεσί ‘in his wits’ (ἐνί with the epic dative plural φρεσί, and οἱ the dative pronoun ‘his’), and ἐτόλμα is the imperfect of τολμάω ‘dare, endure’. θυμός is ‘heart’ here.

sentences.t: τοῖσι δὲ καὶ μετέειπεν ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν Ἀγαμέμνων·
sentences.tr: toisi de kai meteeipen anax andrōn Agamemnōn·
sentences.l: And among them spoke also the lord of men, Agamemnon:
sentences.i: And Agamemnon, lord of men, also spoke among them:
sentences.n: A whole-line speech introduction, as at 3.455 and elsewhere. ἄναξ ἀνδρῶν ‘lord of men’ is Agamemnon’s title, translated every time, and καὶ μετέειπεν ‘spoke also among them’ is the same as the verb at 219, with the movable -ν.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδη Διόμηδες ἐμῷ κεχαρισμένε θυμῷ
τὸν μὲν δὴ ἕταρόν γ’ αἱρήσεαι ὅν κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα,
sentences.tr:
Tydeïdē Diomēdes emōi kecharismene thymōi
ton men dē hetaron g’ hairēseai hon k’ ethelēistha,
sentences.l:
“Tydeus’-son Diomedes, made welcome to my heart,
the companion, indeed, you will choose whom you wish,
sentences.i: “Diomedes, son of Tydeus, dear to my heart, you shall choose as your companion whomever you wish,
sentences.n: Line 234 is word for word the line that opens an earlier address to Diomedes (iliad-029), and the English follows that unit’s. Τυδεΐδη Διόμηδες is the vocative of the name and the patronymic ‘Tydeus’ son’, and κεχαρισμένε is the vocative of the perfect passive participle of χαρίζομαι ‘show favour’, ‘made welcome, dear’. In 235 τὸν … ἕταρον is the object, ‘the companion’, and αἱρήσεαι is the future middle of αἱρέω ‘choose’ (an uncontracted -εαι); ὅν κ’ ἐθέλῃσθα is the relative clause with κε and the subjunctive, ‘whom you may wish’ (ἐθέλῃσθα with the old ending -σθα).

sentences.t: φαινομένων τὸν ἄριστον, ἐπεὶ μεμάασί γε πολλοί.
sentences.tr: phainomenōn ton ariston, epei memaasi ge polloi.
sentences.l: of those who show themselves, the best one, since many are eager.
sentences.i: of those who show themselves, the best, since many are eager.
sentences.n: φαινομένων is a partitive genitive plural, the participle of φαίνομαι ‘show oneself, come forward’: the best ‘of those who show themselves’. τὸν ἄριστον ‘the best’ is the accusative in apposition to τὸν ἕταρον of line 235. μεμάασι is the perfect of μαίομαι ‘be eager’, third plural, and πολλοί is ‘many’.

sentences.t:
μηδὲ σύ γ’ αἰδόμενος σῇσι φρεσὶ τὸν μὲν ἀρείω
καλλείπειν,
sentences.tr:
mēde sy g’ aidomenos sēisi phresi ton men areiō
kalleipein,
sentences.l:
And do not, you, showing respect in your wits, the better man
leave behind,
sentences.i: And do not, out of respect, leave the better man behind,
sentences.n: μηδέ … καλλείπειν: the infinitive καλλείπειν (= καταλείπειν) ‘leave behind’ is used as a command after μηδέ ‘and not’, which is allowed in Homer. αἰδόμενος is the participle of αἰδέομαι ‘feel respect’, and σῇσι φρεσί ‘in your wits’ uses the dative with the ending -σι. τὸν μὲν ἀρείω ‘the one who is better’ has ἀρείω as the accusative singular of ἀρείων (= ἀρείονα) ‘better’, which the next line sets against χείρον’ ‘worse’. The unit ends where the verb ends.

sentences.t:
σὺ δὲ χείρον’ ὀπάσσεαι αἰδοῖ εἴκων
ἐς γενεὴν ὁρόων,
sentences.tr:
sy de cheiron’ opasseai aidoi eikōn
es geneēn horoōn,
sentences.l:
and the worse take along, to respect yielding,
looking to birth,
sentences.i: and take along the worse man, yielding to respect and looking to birth,
sentences.n: σὺ δὲ χείρον’ ὀπάσσεαι: χείρον’ is χείρονα ‘the worse’, and ὀπάσσεαι is the second person of ὀπάζομαι ‘take as a follower’, in a form that can be read as a future; the construction is loose, because the negative of the line before seems to reach over this verb too (‘do not leave the better and take the worse’). αἰδοῖ εἴκων is ‘yielding to respect’ (αἰδοῖ the dative of αἰδώς, and εἴκω ‘yield’), and ἐς γενεὴν ὁρόων is ‘looking to birth’, which means to his rank. The unit ends at the comma after ὁρόων.

sentences.t: μηδ’ εἰ βασιλεύτερός ἐστιν.
sentences.tr: mēd’ ei basileuteros estin.
sentences.l: not even if he is the more kingly.”
sentences.i: not even if he is of higher rank.”
sentences.n: μηδ’ εἰ βασιλεύτερός ἐστιν: μηδ’ ‘not even’, and βασιλεύτερος is the comparative of βασιλεύς ‘king’, ‘more kingly’. The words do not name Menelaus, but the line after the speech says it is for him that Agamemnon feared. The speech ends at the full stop.

sentences.t: ὣς ἔφατ’, ἔδεισεν δὲ περὶ ξανθῷ Μενελάῳ.
sentences.tr: hōs ephat’, edeisen de peri xanthōi Menelaōi.
sentences.l: So he spoke, and he feared for fair-haired Menelaus.
sentences.i: So he spoke, and he was afraid for fair-haired Menelaus.
sentences.n: ὣς ἔφατ’ ‘so he spoke’ is the speech-closing formula, and the second half says what moved Agamemnon: ἔδεισεν δὲ περί … ‘and he feared for’ (περί with the dative ‘for’), with ξανθῷ Μενελάῳ ‘fair-haired Menelaus’ in the dative (Μενελάῳ is the epic form). The reason for his speech is that he did not want his brother taken. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t: τοῖς δ’ αὖτις μετέειπε βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: tois d’ autis meteeipe boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: And among them again spoke Diomedes, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: Diomedes, good at the war-cry, spoke among them again:
sentences.n: A whole-line speech introduction, with αὖτις ‘again’ because Diomedes is speaking a second time. The verb is the aorist μετέειπε, and the epithet is the usual βοὴν ἀγαθός.

sentences.t: εἰ μὲν δὴ ἕταρόν γε κελεύετέ μ’ αὐτὸν ἑλέσθαι,
sentences.tr: ei men dē hetaron ge keleuete m’ auton helesthai,
sentences.l: “If, indeed, you bid me myself to choose a companion,
sentences.i: “If you tell me to choose my companion myself,
sentences.n: The condition. εἰ μὲν δή ‘if indeed’ opens it, and ἕταρον … ἑλέσθαι ‘to choose a companion’ is the infinitive (aorist middle of αἱρέω), with μ’ αὐτόν ‘me myself’ as the accusative that goes with it. κελεύετε is the plural ‘you bid’, since Agamemnon spoke for the council. Diomedes does not name anyone yet, but turns the question around. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t: πῶς ἂν ἔπειτ’ Ὀδυσῆος ἐγὼ θείοιο λαθοίμην,
sentences.tr: pōs an epeit’ Odysēos egō theioio lathoimēn,
sentences.l: how could I, then, Odysseus the divine forget,
sentences.i: how then could I forget divine Odysseus,
sentences.n: The main clause of the condition. πῶς ἂν … λαθοίμην ‘how could I forget’ is an optative with ἂν (the middle of λανθάνομαι ‘forget’ takes a genitive, here Ὀδυσῆος). θείοιο is the epic genitive of θεῖος ‘divine’, and the English uses ‘divine’ for θεῖος to keep ‘heavenly’ for δῖος. The same line stands at Odyssey 1.65, where Zeus asks it, and the English follows that unit’s.

sentences.t:
οὗ πέρι μὲν πρόφρων κραδίη καὶ θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ
ἐν πάντεσσι πόνοισι,
sentences.tr:
hou peri men prophrōn kradiē kai thymos agēnōr
en pantessi ponoisi,
sentences.l:
whose heart beyond others is ready-minded, and manly spirit,
in all toils,
sentences.i: whose heart is more ready than any man’s, and his proud spirit, in every toil,
sentences.n: οὗ is the genitive of the relative ὅς, ‘whose’, and πέρι is an adverb, ‘beyond others’, ‘above all’. πρόφρων is ‘ready-minded’ and goes with κραδίη ‘heart’, and θυμὸς ἀγήνωρ ‘proud spirit’ is the epithet from line 220. ἐν πάντεσσι πόνοισι ‘in all toils’ is the epic dative plural of πόνος. The unit ends at the comma after πόνοισι.

sentences.t: φιλεῖ δέ ἑ Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη.
sentences.tr: philei de he Pallas Athēnē.
sentences.l: and loves him, Pallas Athena.
sentences.i: and Pallas Athena loves him.
sentences.n: φιλεῖ δέ ἑ: φιλεῖ is ‘loves’ (φιλέω), and ἑ is the enclitic accusative ‘him’. The subject Παλλὰς Ἀθήνη ‘Pallas Athena’ comes at the end, and her love is the reason Odysseus is the man to take. The meaning of Παλλάς is disputed.

sentences.t:
τούτου γ’ ἑσπομένοιο καὶ ἐκ πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο
ἄμφω νοστήσαιμεν,
sentences.tr:
toutou g’ hespomenoio kai ek pyros aithomenoio
amphō nostēsaimen,
sentences.l:
with him following, even out of burning fire
we both could return,
sentences.i: with him to follow us, even out of blazing fire we two could return home,
sentences.n: τούτου γ’ ἑσπομένοιο is a genitive absolute, ‘he following’ (ἑσπομένοιο is the participle of ἕπομαι in the form that keeps the old ἑ-, with the epic ending -οιο). ἐκ πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο ‘out of blazing fire’ names the worst case. ἄμφω νοστήσαιμεν is the aorist optative ‘we both could come home’, and ἄμφω ‘both’ means Diomedes and Odysseus. νοστέω is ‘come home’.

sentences.t: ἐπεὶ περίοιδε νοῆσαι.
sentences.tr: epei perioide noēsai.
sentences.l: since beyond others he knows how to think.”
sentences.i: since he is better than anyone at knowing what to do.”
sentences.n: ἐπεὶ περίοιδε νοῆσαι: περίοιδε is περί ‘beyond’ with οἶδε, the perfect of οἶδα ‘know’ (present in sense), so ‘knows beyond others’, and it takes the infinitive νοῆσαι ‘to think, to plan’. The reason is Odysseus’ quickness of mind. Diomedes’ speech ends here, and he has named his man.

sentences.t: τὸν δ’ αὖτε προσέειπε πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς·
sentences.tr: ton d’ aute proseeipe polytlas dios Odysseus·
sentences.l: Him then in turn addressed much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus:
sentences.i: Then much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus spoke to him in turn:
sentences.n: A whole-line reply-formula, the same as at 9.676. τὸν … προσέειπε ‘addressed him’, αὖτε ‘in turn’, and the name formula πολύτλας δῖος Ὀδυσσεύς ‘much-enduring, heavenly Odysseus’ in the house rendering. The edition begins a new paragraph here.

sentences.t: Τυδεΐδη μήτ’ ἄρ με μάλ’ αἴνεε μήτέ τι νείκει·
sentences.tr: Tydeïdē mēt’ ar me mal’ ainee mēte ti neikei·
sentences.l: “Tydeus’-son, neither praise me too much nor revile me at all;
sentences.i: “Son of Tydeus, do not praise me too much or find fault with me at all;
sentences.n: Τυδεΐδη is the vocative of Τυδεΐδης ‘son of Tydeus’. αἴνεε is the second singular present imperative of αἰνέω ‘praise’ (uncontracted, so the e-ending shows), and νείκει is the imperative of νεικέω ‘revile’; the two are joined by μήτ’ … μήτε ‘neither … nor’. μάλ’ ‘very much’ goes with αἴνεε, and τι ‘at all’ with νείκει. Odysseus refuses both praise and blame as beside the point.

sentences.t: εἰδόσι γάρ τοι ταῦτα μετ’ Ἀργείοις ἀγορεύεις.
sentences.tr: eidosi gar toi tauta met’ Argeiois agoreueis.
sentences.l: for to those who know, you see, these things you declare among the Argives.
sentences.i: for you are saying this among Argives who know it already.
sentences.n: εἰδόσι is the dative plural of the participle of οἶδα ‘know’; the Argives are those who know. τοι is the particle ‘you see’ (not the pronoun), μετ’ Ἀργείοις is ‘among the Argives’, and ἀγορεύεις is ‘you declare’ (ἀγορεύω keeps ‘declare’ for a public pronouncement). Odysseus means that everyone has seen what he can do, so there is no need to tell them.

sentences.t: ἀλλ’ ἴομεν·
sentences.tr: all’ iomen·
sentences.l: But let us go;
sentences.i: But come, let us go;
sentences.n: ἀλλ’ ἴομεν: ἴομεν is the first person plural subjunctive of εἶμι ‘go’ with the short vowel of the Homeric subjunctive, used as an exhortation, ‘let us go’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after ἴομεν, in the middle of the line, and the reason follows.

sentences.t: μάλα γὰρ νὺξ ἄνεται, ἐγγύθι δ’ ἠώς,
sentences.tr: mala gar nyx anetai, engythi d’ ēōs,
sentences.l: for very much the night is being spent, and near is the dawn,
sentences.i: for the night is far spent, and dawn is near,
sentences.n: μάλα γὰρ νὺξ ἄνεται: ἄνεται is generally taken as a form of ἀνύω ‘finish, accomplish’, so ‘is being spent’, but the form is unusual and the sense is the usual explanation, not certain. ἐγγύθι δ’ ἠώς ‘and near is the dawn’ uses ἐγγύθι (= ἐγγύς) ‘near’ and ἠώς ‘dawn’. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t: ἄστρα δὲ δὴ προβέβηκε,
sentences.tr: astra de dē probebēke,
sentences.l: and the stars have advanced,
sentences.i: the stars have moved on,
sentences.n: ἄστρα δὲ δὴ προβέβηκε: ἄστρα is the plural of ἄστρον ‘star’, and its verb is singular, as usual with a neuter plural; προβέβηκε is the perfect of προβαίνω ‘go forward’. The perfect says that they have advanced and are now far along. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
παροίχωκεν δὲ πλέων νὺξ
τῶν δύο μοιράων,
sentences.tr:
paroichōken de pleōn nyx
tōn dyo moiraōn,
sentences.l:
and gone by is the night,
more than the two parts,
sentences.i: and the night has run on past its two parts,
sentences.n: παροίχωκεν is the perfect of παροίχομαι ‘go by, be past’, and πλέων is ‘more’, agreeing with νύξ ‘night’. τῶν δύο μοιράων ‘the two parts’ is a genitive whose construction is disputed (‘more than’ the two parts, or ‘further on’ among them); the sense is clear from the next line, that the night has three parts and two are gone. The unit ends at the comma after μοιράων.

sentences.t: τριτάτη δ’ ἔτι μοῖρα λέλειπται.
sentences.tr: tritatē d’ eti moira leleiptai.
sentences.l: and the third part is still left.”
sentences.i: and the third part is still left.”
sentences.n: τριτάτη δ’ ἔτι μοῖρα λέλειπται: τριτάτη is the epic form of τρίτη ‘third’, and λέλειπται is the perfect passive of λείπω ‘leave’, so ‘is left’. Odysseus ends his speech with the shortage of time.

sentences.t: ὣς εἰπόνθ’ ὅπλοισιν ἔνι δεινοῖσιν ἐδύτην.
sentences.tr: hōs eiponth’ hoploisin eni deinoisin edytēn.
sentences.l: So having spoken, in dread arms the two clad themselves.
sentences.i: So they spoke, and the two clad themselves in their dread arms.
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph here, as the arming begins. ὣς εἰπόνθ’ is ὣς εἰπόντε, the dual participle of εἶπον with its ending elided, ‘the two having spoken’. ἐδύτην is the dual aorist of δύω ‘get into, put on’, with ὅπλοισιν ἔνι δεινοῖσιν ‘in dread arms’, where ἔνι is ἐν standing between the noun and its adjective. δεινός is ‘dread’, the house rendering. From ὅπλοισιν on, the line is the same as in 272.

sentences.t:
Τυδεΐδῃ μὲν δῶκε μενεπτόλεμος Θρασυμήδης
φάσγανον ἄμφηκες·
sentences.tr:
Tydeïdēi men dōke meneptolemos Thrasymēdēs
phasganon amphēkes·
sentences.l:
To Tydeus’-son gave steadfast-in-battle Thrasymedes
a two-edged sword;
sentences.i: Thrasymedes, steadfast in battle, gave Tydeus’ son a two-edged sword;
sentences.n: Τυδεΐδῃ is the dative of Τυδεΐδης ‘Tydeus’ son’, and δῶκε is the aorist of δίδωμι ‘give’. μενεπτόλεμος ‘steadfast in battle’ is the stock epithet of Thrasymedes, the house rendering; Thrasymedes is one of Nestor’s sons (at 3.442 of the Odyssey he is ‘steadfast in battle’ too). φάσγανον ἄμφηκες ‘a two-edged sword’ has ἄμφηκες ‘two-edged’, an adjective of two endings. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after ἄμφηκες.

sentences.t: τὸ δ’ ἑὸν παρὰ νηῒ λέλειπτο·
sentences.tr: to d’ heon para nēï leleipto·
sentences.l: for his own had been left by the ship;
sentences.i: for his own had been left by the ship;
sentences.n: τὸ δ’ ἑὸν παρὰ νηῒ λέλειπτο: τὸ ἑόν is ‘his own (sword)’, with ἑός the possessive ‘own’, and νηῒ is the dative of ναῦς ‘by the ship’. λέλειπτο is the pluperfect passive of λείπω ‘had been left’, without the augment. The reason Diomedes needs a loan is that his own sword had been left behind. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after λέλειπτο.

sentences.t: καὶ σάκος·
sentences.tr: kai sakos·
sentences.l: and a shield;
sentences.i: and a shield;
sentences.n: καὶ σάκος: the shield is a second gift, with σάκος ‘shield’ as the object of the same verb, δῶκε, carried from the line before. The unit is short because it ends at the raised dot (·) in the middle of the line.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ κυνέην κεφαλῆφιν ἔθηκε
ταυρείην,
sentences.tr:
amphi de hoi kyneēn kephalēphin ethēke
taureiēn,
sentences.l:
and around his head a helmet he put,
of bull’s hide,
sentences.i: and set a helmet of bull’s hide about his head,
sentences.n: ἀμφὶ … ἔθηκε is a split compound (tmesis for ἀμφέθηκε) ‘put around’; οἱ is the dative ‘on him’ and κεφαλῆφιν is an epic form in -φιν, ‘on the head’. κυνέη is ‘helmet’, usually made of leather or hide. ταυρείην ‘of a bull’ is an adjective in the accusative, agreeing with κυνέην, so the helmet is made of bull’s hide. The unit ends at the comma after ταυρείην.

sentences.t:
ἄφαλόν τε καὶ ἄλλοφον, ἥ τε καταῖτυξ
κέκληται,
sentences.tr:
aphalon te kai allophon, hē te kataityx
keklētai,
sentences.l:
ridgeless and crestless, which is called
a kataityx,
sentences.i: without ridge and without crest, the kind that is called a kataityx,
sentences.n: ἄφαλον is ‘ridgeless’ (ἀ- + φάλος ‘ridge of a helmet’, a word whose sense is not certain) and ἄλλοφον is ‘crestless’ (ἀ- + λόφος ‘crest’); the two together describe a plain cap. ἥ τε καταῖτυξ κέκληται means ‘the kind that is called kataityx’, with κέκληται the perfect passive of καλέω; καταῖτυξ is a word whose origin we do not know, and so it is left as the Greek name. The unit ends at the comma after κέκληται.

sentences.t: ῥύεται δὲ κάρη θαλερῶν αἰζηῶν.
sentences.tr: rhyetai de karē thalerōn aizēōn.
sentences.l: and it protects the head of flourishing vigorous young men.
sentences.i: and it protects the heads of flourishing young men.
sentences.n: ῥύεται δὲ κάρη: ῥύεται is ‘protects’ (ῥύομαι), and κάρη is an old word for ‘head’, used as a singular for several heads. θαλερῶν αἰζηῶν ‘of flourishing young men’ is a genitive plural: θαλερός ‘flourishing’ and αἰζηός ‘vigorous young man’. The subject of ῥύεται is the καταῖτυξ, the plain cap.

sentences.t:
Μηριόνης δ’ Ὀδυσῆϊ δίδου βιὸν ἠδὲ φαρέτρην
καὶ ξίφος,
sentences.tr:
Mērionēs d’ Odysēï didou bion ēde pharetrēn
kai xiphos,
sentences.l:
And Meriones to Odysseus gave a bow and a quiver
and a sword,
sentences.i: And Meriones gave Odysseus a bow and a quiver and a sword,
sentences.n: δίδου is the imperfect of δίδωμι ‘give’ (without the augment), ‘was giving’; Ὀδυσῆϊ is the dative of Ὀδυσεύς. βιόν is the accusative of βιός ‘bow’ (the accent tells it from βίος ‘life’), and φαρέτρην is ‘quiver’. ἠδὲ ‘and’ links the three. The unit ends at the comma after ξίφος.

sentences.t:
ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ κυνέην κεφαλῆφιν ἔθηκε
ῥινοῦ ποιητήν·
sentences.tr:
amphi de hoi kyneēn kephalēphin ethēke
rhinou poiētēn·
sentences.l:
and around his head a helmet he put,
made of hide;
sentences.i: and set a helmet about his head, made of hide;
sentences.n: Line 261 from ἀμφὶ δέ οἱ on is the same as 257, and the English follows 257’s. ῥινοῦ ποιητήν is ‘made of hide’: ῥινοῦ is the genitive of ῥινός ‘hide’, and ποιητήν ‘made’ is an adjective in the accusative agreeing with κυνέην. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after ποιητήν.

sentences.t:
πολέσιν δ’ ἔντοσθεν ἱμᾶσιν
ἐντέτατο στερεῶς·
sentences.tr:
polesin d’ entosthen himasin
entetato stereōs·
sentences.l:
and with many straps on the inside
it was stretched firmly;
sentences.i: and inside it was stretched firmly with many straps;
sentences.n: πολέσιν is the epic dative plural of πολύς ‘many’, and ἱμᾶσιν is the dative plural of ἱμάς ‘strap’. ἔντοσθεν ‘on the inside’ (from ἐντός). ἐντέτατο is the pluperfect passive of ἐντείνω ‘stretch in’, with στερεῶς ‘firmly’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after στερεῶς.

sentences.t:
ἔκτοσθε δὲ λευκοὶ ὀδόντες
ἀργιόδοντος ὑὸς θαμέες ἔχον ἔνθα καὶ ἔνθα
εὖ καὶ ἐπισταμένως·
sentences.tr:
ektosthe de leukoi odontes
argiodontos hyos thamees echon entha kai entha
eu kai epistamenōs·
sentences.i: and on the outside the white teeth of a white-toothed boar were set close together, here and there, well and skilfully;
sentences.n: ἔκτοσθε ‘on the outside’ (from ἐκτός) sets the outside against the inside of the line before. ἀργιόδοντος ὑὸς is ‘of a white-toothed boar’ (ἀργός ‘bright, white’ + ὀδών ‘tooth’), and ὑός is the genitive of ὗς, so the tusks are fixed on the helmet. θαμέες is ‘thick-set, close together’ and ἔχον is the imperfect of ἔχω (without the augment) ‘held, kept’. εὖ καὶ ἐπισταμένως ‘well and skilfully’ is two adverbs, the second from ἐπίσταμαι ‘know how’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after ἐπισταμένως.

sentences.t: μέσσῃ δ’ ἐνὶ πῖλος ἀρήρει.
sentences.tr: messēi d’ eni pilos arērei.
sentences.l: and in the middle was fitted felt.
sentences.i: and in the middle was fitted a lining of felt.
sentences.n: μέσσῃ δ’ ἐνὶ πῖλος ἀρήρει: μέσσῃ is a feminine dative, agreeing with an unspoken κυνέῃ ‘in the middle of the helmet’, with ἐνί placed after the noun, and πῖλος is ‘felt’. ἀρήρει is the pluperfect of ἀραρίσκω ‘fit’, used for a state, ‘was fitted’ (as at 3.338).

sentences.t:
τήν ῥά ποτ’ ἐξ Ἐλεῶνος Ἀμύντορος Ὀρμενίδαο
ἐξέλετ’ Αὐτόλυκος πυκινὸν δόμον ἀντιτορήσας,
sentences.tr:
tēn rha pot’ ex Eleōnos Amyntoros Ormenidao
exelet’ Autolykos pykinon domon antitorēsas,
sentences.l:
which once from Eleon, from Amyntor Ormenus’-son,
Autolycus took out, a solid house having broken through,
sentences.i: It was Autolycus who once took it from Eleon, from Amyntor, son of Ormenus, breaking into his solid house;
sentences.n: τήν is the relative ‘which (helmet)’, with ῥά ‘as we know’ and ποτέ ‘once’. Ἐλεών is a town in Boeotia, and Ἀμύντορος Ὀρμενίδαο is ‘from Amyntor, son of Ormenus’ (Ὀρμενίδαο is an epic patronymic genitive). ἐξέλετο is the aorist middle of ἐξαιρέω ‘take out’, and Αὐτόλυκος is the thief, famous for his trickery (and, in the Odyssey, the maternal grandfather of Odysseus). ἀντιτορήσας is the aorist participle of ἀντιτορέω ‘bore through’, with πυκινὸν δόμον ‘a solid house’ (πυκινός is ‘solid’ in the house rendering), that is, he broke in. The unit ends at the comma after ἀντιτορήσας.

sentences.t: Σκάνδειαν δ’ ἄρα δῶκε Κυθηρίῳ Ἀμφιδάμαντι·
sentences.tr: Skandeian d’ ara dōke Kythēriōi Amphidamanti·
sentences.l: and to Scandeia he gave it, to Amphidamas of Cythera;
sentences.i: he took it to Scandeia and gave it to Amphidamas of Cythera;
sentences.n: Σκάνδειαν δ’ ἄρα δῶκε: Σκάνδεια is a place, evidently on or by Cythera, and the accusative is one of direction, ‘to Scandeia’, with a going understood: he took the helmet there and gave it. Κυθηρίῳ Ἀμφιδάμαντι ‘to Cytherian Amphidamas’ is the dative of the receiver, with Κυθήριος ‘of Cythera’ (the island in the south). The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after Ἀμφιδάμαντι, and the gift passes on in the next line.

sentences.t: Ἀμφιδάμας δὲ Μόλῳ δῶκε ξεινήϊον εἶναι,
sentences.tr: Amphidamas de Molōi dōke xeinēïon einai,
sentences.l: and Amphidamas to Molus gave it, to be a guest-gift,
sentences.i: Amphidamas gave it to Molus to be a guest-gift,
sentences.n: Ἀμφιδάμας … Μόλῳ δῶκε ‘Amphidamas gave it to Molus’ continues the chain of owners. ξεινήϊον εἶναι is ‘to be a guest-gift’, with the infinitive εἶναι of purpose (‘to be’) and ξεινήϊον ‘a gift given to a guest’, the same as the Odyssey’s ξεινήιον. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t: αὐτὰρ ὃ Μηριόνῃ δῶκεν ᾧ παιδὶ φορῆναι·
sentences.tr: autar ho Mērionēi dōken hōi paidi phorēnai·
sentences.l: and he to Meriones gave it, his son, to wear;
sentences.i: and he gave it to his son Meriones to wear;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ … δῶκεν: ὃ is the demonstrative ‘he’, meaning Molus. ᾧ παιδί is ‘to his own son’, using ᾧ as the possessive ‘his own’ (ὅς, kept apart from the relative), and Μηριόνῃ is the dative of the name. φορῆναι is the aorist infinitive of φορέω ‘wear’, in a form with the epic ending -ῆναι. This is how Meriones came to own the helmet he now lends. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after φορῆναι.

sentences.t: δὴ τότ’ Ὀδυσσῆος πύκασεν κάρη ἀμφιτεθεῖσα.
sentences.tr: dē tot’ Odyssēos pykasen karē amphitetheisa.
sentences.l: then indeed it covered Odysseus’ head, being put around it.
sentences.i: and now, put round his head, it covered the head of Odysseus.
sentences.n: δὴ τότ’ ‘then indeed’ is the present moment after the history of the helmet. πύκασεν is the aorist of πυκάζω ‘cover closely’, κάρη is the old ‘head’, and Ὀδυσσῆος is the epic genitive. ἀμφιτεθεῖσα is the aorist passive participle of ἀμφιτίθημι ‘put round’, in the feminine, agreeing with the helmet, ‘being put around’. The sentence that told its history ends at the full stop.

sentences.t: τὼ δ’ ἐπεὶ οὖν ὅπλοισιν ἔνι δεινοῖσιν ἐδύτην,
sentences.tr: tō d’ epei oun hoploisin eni deinoisin edytēn,
sentences.l: And the two, when then in dread arms they had clad themselves,
sentences.i: And when the two had clad themselves in their dread arms,
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph here. τὼ is the dual article ‘the two’, ἐδύτην is the dual aorist of δύω ‘get into’, as at 254, and ὅπλοισιν ἔνι δεινοῖσιν ‘in dread arms’ repeats 254’s phrase. ἐπεὶ οὖν is ‘when then’, and the main clause comes in the next line.

sentences.t: βάν ῥ’ ἰέναι, λιπέτην δὲ κατ’ αὐτόθι πάντας ἀρίστους.
sentences.tr: ban rh’ ienai, lipetēn de kat’ autothi pantas aristous.
sentences.l: they set out to go, and left on the spot all the best men.
sentences.i: they set out, and left all the chiefs behind on the spot.
sentences.n: βάν ῥ’ ἰέναι: βάν is the aorist of βαίνω in the plural (epic βάν = ἔβησαν), and ῥ’ is ῥά, with the infinitive ἰέναι ‘to go’ (an infinitive of purpose with a verb of motion), so ‘they set out to go’. λιπέτην is the dual aorist of λείπω ‘leave’, and the dual returns to the two. κατ’ αὐτόθι is ‘on the spot’, and πάντας ἀρίστους ‘all the best men’ are the chiefs of the council, left where they had sat.

sentences.t:
τοῖσι δὲ δεξιὸν ἧκεν ἐρῳδιὸν ἐγγὺς ὁδοῖο
Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη·
sentences.tr:
toisi de dexion hēken erōidion engys hodoio
Pallas Athēnaiē·
sentences.l:
And on the right a heron sent them, near the road,
Pallas Athena;
sentences.i: And Pallas Athena sent them a heron on their right, near the road;
sentences.n: τοῖσι ‘to them’ is the dative of the two men. δεξιόν ‘on the right’ was a lucky side for an omen, and ἐρῳδιόν is ‘a heron’ (accusative); ἧκεν is the aorist of ἵημι ‘send’, and ὁδοῖο is the epic genitive of ὁδός ‘road’, with ἐγγύς ‘near’. Παλλὰς Ἀθηναίη ‘Pallas Athena’ is a variant of the usual Ἀθήνη. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after Ἀθηναίη.

sentences.t:
τοὶ δ’ οὐκ ἴδον ὀφθαλμοῖσι
νύκτα δι’ ὀρφναίην,
sentences.tr:
toi d’ ouk idon ophthalmoisi
nykta di’ orphnaiēn,
sentences.l:
and they did not see it with their eyes
through the murky night,
sentences.i: and they did not see it with their eyes through the murky night,
sentences.n: τοὶ δ’ ‘but they’ is the two men. ἴδον is the aorist of ὁράω ‘see’, without the augment, and ὀφθαλμοῖσι is the dative plural (epic -οισι) of ὀφθαλμός ‘eye’. νύκτα δι’ ὀρφναίην is διά with the accusative, ‘through the murky night’; ὀρφναῖος is ‘murky, dark’. The unit ends at the comma after ὀρφναίην.

sentences.t: ἀλλὰ κλάγξαντος ἄκουσαν.
sentences.tr: alla klanxantos akousan.
sentences.l: but heard it as it shrieked.
sentences.i: but they heard it shriek.
sentences.n: ἀλλὰ κλάγξαντος ἄκουσαν: ἀλλά ‘but’ sets hearing against sight. κλάγξαντος is the aorist participle of κλάζω ‘shriek, cry’, in the genitive, and ἄκουσαν is the aorist (ἤκουσαν, without the augment) of ἀκούω ‘hear’, which takes a genitive for the thing heard; the participle agrees with an unspoken ‘the bird’. So they know the omen from the cry.

sentences.t: χαῖρε δὲ τῷ ὄρνιθ’ Ὀδυσεύς, ἠρᾶτο δ’ Ἀθήνῃ·
sentences.tr: chaire de tōi ornith’ Odyseus, ērato d’ Athēnēi·
sentences.l: And he rejoiced at the bird, Odysseus, and prayed to Athena:
sentences.i: Odysseus was glad of the bird, and prayed to Athena:
sentences.n: χαῖρε is the imperfect of χαίρω ‘rejoice’, and τῷ ὄρνιθ’ is the dative τῷ ὄρνιθι ‘at the bird’, with its ending elided. ἠρᾶτο is the imperfect of ἀράομαι ‘pray’. Odysseus takes the heron as a good sign and prays to the goddess who sent it. The line ends at the raised dot (·), and his prayer follows.

sentences.t:
κλῦθί μευ αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος, ἥ τέ μοι αἰεὶ
ἐν πάντεσσι πόνοισι παρίστασαι,
sentences.tr:
klythi meu aigiochoio Dios tekos, hē te moi aiei
en pantessi ponoisi paristasai,
sentences.l:
“Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, you who always
in all toils stand by me,
sentences.i: “Hear me, child of aegis-bearing Zeus, you who always stand by me in all my toils,
sentences.n: κλῦθί μευ: κλῦθι is the aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, and μευ is the epic genitive of ἐγώ (the genitive goes with κλύω), ‘hear me’. αἰγιόχοιο Διὸς τέκος is ‘child of aegis-bearing Zeus’, the house form. ἥ τέ μοι αἰεί … παρίστασαι: ἥ is the relative ‘who’, and παρίστασαι is the second person singular of παρίσταμαι ‘stand beside’, here ‘you stand by me’; ἐν πάντεσσι πόνοισι is ‘in all toils’, and the unit ends at the comma after παρίστασαι.

sentences.t:
οὐδέ σε λήθω
κινύμενος·
sentences.tr:
oude se lēthō
kinymenos·
sentences.l:
and I do not escape your notice
as I move;
sentences.i: and I never escape your notice whenever I move;
sentences.n: οὐδέ σε λήθω: λήθω is ‘I escape the notice of’ (λανθάνω) and takes σε in the accusative, so ‘I am not hidden from you’. κινύμενος is the participle of κίνυμαι ‘move, stir’, ‘moving about’, and the idea is that Athena is aware of him wherever he goes. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after κινύμενος.

sentences.t: νῦν αὖτε μάλιστά με φῖλαι Ἀθήνη,
sentences.tr: nyn aute malista me philai Athēnē,
sentences.l: now again most of all love me, Athena,
sentences.i: now again show your love for me most of all, Athena,
sentences.n: νῦν αὖτε μάλιστα ‘now again most of all’ asks for her love this time more than before. φῖλαι is read as an aorist imperative of φιλέω ‘love’, ‘show your love to me’ (the ending and the formation are uncertain), and με is the object. Ἀθήνη is the vocative. The unit ends at the comma.

sentences.t:
δὸς δὲ πάλιν ἐπὶ νῆας ἐϋκλεῖας ἀφικέσθαι
ῥέξαντας μέγα ἔργον, ὅ κε Τρώεσσι μελήσῃ.
sentences.tr:
dos de palin epi nēas eÿkleias aphikesthai
rhexantas mega ergon, ho ke Trōessi melēsēi.
sentences.l:
and grant that to the well-famed ships we come back again,
having done a great deed, which will be a care to the Trojans.”
sentences.i: and grant that we may come back to the ships of good name after doing some great deed that will trouble the Trojans.”
sentences.n: δός is the aorist imperative of δίδωμι ‘give, grant’, followed by ἀφικέσθαι ‘to arrive’. πάλιν ἐπὶ νῆας ἐϋκλεῖας is ‘back to the ships of good name’ (ἐϋκλεής, the house rendering ‘of good name’). ῥέξαντας ‘having done’ is the aorist participle of ῥέζω, accusative plural for the two men, with μέγα ἔργον ‘a great deed’ as its object. ὅ κε Τρώεσσι μελήσῃ is a relative clause with the subjunctive, ‘which will be a care to the Trojans’, and μέλω ‘be a care’ takes the dative. Line 281 is metrically irregular as transmitted: in the scansion made, the final syllable of πάλιν before ἐπί and that of ἐϋκλεῖας before ἀφικέσθαι are short by nature yet stand where a long is needed, and the scanner finds a second scansion of equal cost.

sentences.t: δεύτερος αὖτ’ ἠρᾶτο βοὴν ἀγαθὸς Διομήδης·
sentences.tr: deuteros aut’ ērato boēn agathos Diomēdēs·
sentences.l: Second in turn prayed Diomedes, good at the war-cry:
sentences.i: Diomedes, good at the war-cry, prayed second in his turn:
sentences.n: The edition begins a new paragraph here. δεύτερος αὖτ’ ἠρᾶτο ‘second, in turn, prayed’ marks the order of the two prayers, and the speaker is named with the stock βοὴν ἀγαθός. The line ends at the raised dot (·), and the prayer follows.

sentences.t: κέκλυθι νῦν καὶ ἐμεῖο Διὸς τέκος Ἀτρυτώνη·
sentences.tr: keklythi nyn kai emeio Dios tekos Atrytōnē·
sentences.l: “Hear me too now, child of Zeus, Atrytone;
sentences.i: “Hear me now as well, child of Zeus, Atrytone;
sentences.n: κέκλυθι is the reduplicated aorist imperative of κλύω ‘hear’, and ἐμεῖο is the epic genitive of ἐγώ, ‘hear me’; καὶ ἐμεῖο ‘me too’ adds that he asks as Odysseus did. Διὸς τέκος Ἀτρυτώνη ‘child of Zeus, Atrytone’ is a title of Athena; Ἀτρυτώνη is traditionally ‘the Unwearied’, but the formation is irregular and the sense is not certain, so the Greek is left as a name. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after Ἀτρυτώνη.

sentences.t:
σπεῖό μοι ὡς ὅτε πατρὶ ἅμ’ ἕσπεο Τυδέϊ δίῳ
ἐς Θήβας,
sentences.tr:
speio moi hōs hote patri ham’ hespeo Tydeï diōi
es Thēbas,
sentences.l:
go with me as when with my father you went,
with Tydeus the heavenly, to Thebes,
sentences.i: go with me as you went with my father, heavenly Tydeus, to Thebes,
sentences.n: σπεῖο is the aorist imperative middle of ἕπομαι ‘follow’, and σπεῖό μοι ‘go with me’ is a prayer that she attend him as she had his father. ἕσπεο is the aorist second person of the same verb, ‘you went with’, with πατρί … Τυδέϊ δίῳ ‘my father, heavenly Tydeus’ as the dative (δίῳ is ‘heavenly’, the house rendering of δῖος). ἐς Θήβας is ‘to Thebes’, and Tydeus’ embassy there is the story that Agamemnon told at 4.372 ff. The unit ends at the comma after Θήβας.

sentences.t: ὅτε τε πρὸ Ἀχαιῶν ἄγγελος ᾔει.
sentences.tr: hote te pro Achaiōn angelos ēiei.
sentences.l: when as a messenger he went before the Achaeans.
sentences.i: when he went as a messenger on behalf of the Achaeans.
sentences.n: ὅτε τε … ᾔει: ᾔει is the imperfect of εἶμι ‘go’, in the form that keeps its old augment, ‘he went’. πρὸ Ἀχαιῶν is ‘on behalf of the Achaeans’ (πρό with the genitive ‘for’), or ‘ahead of them’, and ἄγγελος is ‘messenger’. The unit ends at the full stop, and the story goes on in the next lines.

sentences.t: τοὺς δ’ ἄρ’ ἐπ’ Ἀσωπῷ λίπε χαλκοχίτωνας Ἀχαιούς,
sentences.tr: tous d’ ar’ ep’ Asōpōi lipe chalkochitōnas Achaious,
sentences.l: Them he left by the Asopus, the bronze-shirted Achaeans,
sentences.i: He left the bronze-shirted Achaeans at the Asopus,
sentences.n: τοὺς δ’ ἄρ’ … λίπε ‘them he left’, with the object τοὺς … Ἀχαιούς, and λίπε the aorist of λείπω ‘leave’ (without the augment). χαλκοχίτωνας is the house ‘bronze-shirted’. ἐπ’ Ἀσωπῷ is ‘at the Asopus’, a river near Thebes (in Boeotia); ἐπί with the dative gives the place.

sentences.t:
αὐτὰρ ὃ μειλίχιον μῦθον φέρε Καδμείοισι
κεῖσ’·
sentences.tr:
autar ho meilichion mython phere Kadmeioisi
keis’·
sentences.l:
but he a gentle word carried to the Cadmeans
there;
sentences.i: but he carried a gentle word to the Cadmeans there;
sentences.n: αὐτὰρ ὃ … φέρε: ὃ is the demonstrative ‘he’ (Tydeus), and φέρε is the imperfect of φέρω ‘carry’ without the augment. μειλίχιον μῦθον is ‘a gentle word’, the adjective being the house rendering of μειλίχιος, and Καδμείοισι is the epic dative plural of Καδμεῖοι ‘Cadmeans’ (the Thebans, descended from Cadmus). κεῖσε is ‘there’ (to there), elided as κεῖσ’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after κεῖσ’.

sentences.t:
ἀτὰρ ἂψ ἀπιὼν μάλα μέρμερα μήσατο ἔργα
σὺν σοὶ δῖα θεά, ὅτε οἱ πρόφρασσα παρέστης.
sentences.tr:
atar aps apiōn mala mermera mēsato erga
syn soi dia thea, hote hoi prophrassa parestēs.
sentences.l:
but going back, very baneful deeds he devised
with you, heavenly goddess, when ready-minded you stood by him.
sentences.i: but on his way back he devised very baneful deeds with your help, heavenly goddess, when you stood by him with a ready mind.
sentences.n: ἀτὰρ ἂψ ἀπιών: ἀτάρ ‘but’, ἂψ ‘back’, and ἀπιών the participle of ἄπειμι ‘go away’, so ‘going back’. μάλα μέρμερα … ἔργα is ‘very baneful deeds’ (μέρμερα, an adjective whose origin is uncertain, is kept as ‘baneful’), and μήσατο is the aorist middle of μήδομαι ‘devise’. σὺν σοί δῖα θεά: δῖα is ‘heavenly’, feminine, and θεά is ‘goddess’; σὺν σοί ‘with you’ means with her help. ὅτε οἱ πρόφρασσα παρέστης: πρόφρασσα is the feminine of πρόφρων ‘ready-minded’ (the house rendering), οἱ is ‘by him’ (the dative of the pronoun), and παρέστης is the second person aorist of παρίσταμαι ‘stand beside’. Line 289 has no stop at its end, so the two lines make one unit.

sentences.t: ὣς νῦν μοι ἐθέλουσα παρίσταο καί με φύλασσε.
sentences.tr: hōs nyn moi ethelousa paristao kai me phylasse.
sentences.l: So now to me, being willing, stand by, and guard me.
sentences.i: So now be willing to stand by me, and guard me.
sentences.n: ὣς νῦν ‘so now’ asks that she do the same again. ἐθέλουσα is ‘willing’, the present participle of ἐθέλω in the feminine, and παρίσταο is the present imperative middle (second person) of παρίσταμαι ‘stand by’, with the old ending -ο. καί με φύλασσε is ‘and guard me’, with φύλασσε an imperative of φυλάσσω.

sentences.t:
σοὶ δ’ αὖ ἐγὼ ῥέξω βοῦν ἦνιν εὐρυμέτωπον
ἀδμήτην, ἣν οὔ πω ὑπὸ ζυγὸν ἤγαγεν ἀνήρ·
sentences.tr:
soi d’ au egō rhexō boun ēnin eurymetōpon
admētēn, hēn ou pō hypo zygon ēgagen anēr·
sentences.l:
and to you in turn I will sacrifice a yearling heifer, broad-browed,
unbroken, which never yet under the yoke has a man led;
sentences.i: and in return I will sacrifice to you a yearling heifer, broad of brow and unbroken, one that no man has yet led under the yoke;
sentences.n: The two lines repeat, word for word, Nestor’s vow to Athena in the Odyssey (3.382–384), and the English is the same as there. σοὶ δ’ αὖ ἐγὼ ῥέξω: ῥέξω is the future of ῥέζω ‘do, sacrifice’, and αὖ ‘in turn’ means that her help will be repaid. βοῦν ἦνιν is ‘a yearling heifer’ (ἦνις is a word for a young cow), with the adjectives εὐρυμέτωπον ‘broad-browed’ and ἀδμήτην ‘unbroken’ (ἀ- + δαμάω ‘tame’). ἣν οὔ πω ὑπὸ ζυγὸν ἤγαγεν ἀνήρ is ‘which no man has yet led under the yoke’. The unit ends at the raised dot (·) after ἀνήρ.

sentences.t: τήν τοι ἐγὼ ῥέξω χρυσὸν κέρασιν περιχεύας.
sentences.tr: tēn toi egō rhexō chryson kerasin pericheuas.
sentences.l: Her I will sacrifice to you, gold around her horns having poured.”
sentences.i: I will sacrifice her to you, with gold poured around her horns.”
sentences.n: τήν τοι ἐγὼ ῥέξω: τήν is ‘her’, the heifer, and τοι is the epic ‘to you’, the dative of σοί. χρυσὸν κέρασιν περιχεύας is ‘gold around her horns having poured’, where the aorist participle of περιχέω (with its epic spelling) takes χρυσόν as its object and κέρασιν as the dative of the thing covered. The gilding of the horns is a rich vow. Diomedes’ prayer, and this part, end here.
